title: Homes in Hot Places and Cold Places
bigQuestion: How do people build homes that fit where they live?

story.title: Moving Day in Mongolia
story.kicker: Come to the wide, grassy land of Mongolia. A boy helps his family pack up their round home.
paragraphs: Bat wakes up early. The grass near his home is short now. The sheep and goats have eaten it. Today his family will move to new grass. They will take their home with them.
Their home is a ger. It is round like a big drum. Thick felt covers the outside. Felt is a warm cloth made from sheep wool. Inside, wood poles hold up the roof.
Bat helps Dad roll up the felt. Mom ties the poles in a bundle. His sister packs the pots. They load it all onto a truck. In a few hours, the home is packed.
At the new place, they build the ger again. The stove goes in the middle. Bat puts his bed by the wall. The land is new. The home is the same. Bat feels safe.
story.think: Bat's family takes their home with them. What would you pack first from your home?

sections.title: Homes in Cities and by Water

lessons.title: Apartments in Big Cities
lessons.mainIdea: In big cities, many families live in tall buildings called apartments.
reading: Yuki lives in Tokyo, a big city in Japan. Her home is on the tenth floor. She rides an elevator up. From her window, she sees many other tall buildings.
Yuki lives in an *apartment*. An apartment is a home inside a bigger building. Many families live in one building. Each family has its own door.
Big cities have lots of people and not much land. So people build up, not out. Tokyo and New York have many apartments. So does Chicago.

words.d: a home inside a bigger building where many families live
a big place where many people live and work close together

look.title: The Tall Building
look.text: Look at the tall building. It has many windows. Behind one window, a man cooks. Behind another, two kids play a game. Up high, a grandma waters flowers on a small balcony. Every window is a different home.
look.prompt: How many homes might be in this one building? How can you tell?

check.q: Where does Yuki live?
check.why: Yuki lives on the tenth floor of a building in Tokyo. That is an apartment.

check.q: Why do big cities build tall buildings?
choices: There are many people and not much land
Tall buildings are warmer than all others
check.why: The reading says cities have lots of people and not much land, so they build up.

check.q: What is an apartment?
choices: A home inside a bigger building
check.why: The reading says an apartment is a home inside a bigger building.

lessons.title: Houses on Stilts
lessons.mainIdea: Near water, some houses stand up high on poles to stay dry.
reading: Niran lives in Thailand, near a river. In the rainy season, the river gets high. Water spreads over the ground. But Niran's floor stays dry.
His house stands on *stilts*. Stilts are tall, strong poles. They hold the house up above the ground. Water can flow under the house.
Stilt houses are found in many wet places. The space under the house is useful too. It can be shady. Families may keep a boat there.

words.d: tall, strong poles that hold a house up off the ground
a lot of water that covers land that is usually dry

look.title: Rainy Season
look.text: Look at the house on tall poles. It rained all week. Brown water fills the yard. A small boat floats under the house. Up on the porch, a girl sits dry. She waves at a neighbor rowing by.
look.prompt: What keeps the girl dry? What would happen to a house with no stilts?

check.q: What holds up Niran's house?
check.why: Niran's house stands on stilts, tall poles that hold it up.

check.q: Why do people near water use stilts?
choices: To keep the house dry when water rises
check.why: The reading says water can flow under the house, so the floor stays dry.

check.q: What country does Niran live in?
check.why: The reading says Niran lives in Thailand, near a river.

sections.title: Homes in Dry Lands and Open Grass

lessons.title: Adobe Homes
lessons.mainIdea: In hot, dry places, thick mud-brick walls keep a home cool.
reading: Eva lives in New Mexico. The sun is hot. There is little rain. Her home has thick, brown walls. Inside, it feels cool.
The walls are made of *adobe*. Adobe is a brick made of mud and straw. People dry the bricks in the sun. Pueblo people in New Mexico built with adobe long ago.
Thick adobe walls warm up slowly in the day. So the inside stays cool. At night, the walls give back warmth. Many people still build this way.

words.d: a brick made of mud and straw, dried in the sun
with very little rain or water

look.title: Making Bricks
look.text: Look at the rows of mud bricks on the ground. A man mixes mud, water, and straw. He presses it into a wood box. He lifts the box. A brick sits in the hot sun. After many days, it is hard.
look.prompt: What does the sun do to the bricks? Why is that helpful in a dry place?

check.q: What is adobe made of?
check.why: The reading says adobe is a brick made of mud and straw.

check.q: How does Eva's home feel inside on a hot day?
check.why: Thick adobe walls warm up slowly, so the inside stays cool.

check.q: Where does Eva live?
check.why: The reading says Eva lives in New Mexico, where it is hot and dry.

lessons.title: The Ger That Moves
lessons.mainIdea: Herders in Mongolia live in gers, round homes they can take with them.
reading: Bat's family are *herders*. Herders take care of animals like sheep, goats, and horses. The animals need fresh grass. So the family moves to find it.
Their home is a ger. Some people call it a yurt. It has a wood frame and thick felt walls. The felt keeps out cold wind. A stove in the middle keeps it warm.
A ger can be taken down and put up again. That is why it works for families who move. Many Mongolian families still live in gers.

words.d: a person who takes care of animals like sheep, goats, or horses
a round home with a wood frame and felt walls, used in Mongolia; also called a yurt

look.title: Inside the Ger
look.text: Look inside the round ger. A stove sits in the middle. Its pipe goes up through a hole in the roof. Beds line the round wall. A bright rug covers the floor. Outside, wind blows hard. Inside, it is warm.
look.prompt: Why is the stove in the middle? What keeps the wind out?

check.q: Why does Bat's family move?
check.why: The reading says the animals need fresh grass, so the family moves to find it.

check.q: What is another name for a ger?
check.why: The reading says some people call a ger a yurt.

check.q: What keeps a ger warm?
check.why: The felt keeps out cold wind, and the stove in the middle keeps it warm.

sections.title: Cold Lands and What Every Home Needs

lessons.title: Snow-Block Shelters
lessons.mainIdea: Long ago, Inuit hunters built warm shelters out of snow blocks.
reading: The Inuit live in the far north, in lands of ice and snow. Long ago, some Inuit hunters traveled far in winter. They needed a shelter for the night.
They cut hard snow into blocks. They stacked the blocks in a round dome. This snow house is often called an *igloo*. The word means house in their language.
Snow can hold in warmth. Inside, a small lamp made it warmer. Today, most Inuit live in wood houses. Some still know how to build with snow.

words.d: a dome-shaped shelter made of snow blocks, once built by some Inuit hunters
a place that keeps you safe from wind, rain, cold, or sun

look.title: The Snow Dome
look.text: Look at the white dome on the snow. Blocks go round and round. Each row leans in a little. At the top, one block closes the dome. A small door is low to the ground. Outside it is very cold. Inside, the wind cannot reach.
look.prompt: Why do you think the door is so low?

check.q: What did Inuit hunters use to build winter shelters?
check.why: The reading says they cut hard snow into blocks and stacked them in a dome.

check.q: Where do most Inuit live today?
check.why: The reading says today most Inuit live in wood houses.

check.q: What is a shelter?
choices: A place that keeps you safe from wind and cold
check.why: A shelter keeps you safe from wind, rain, cold, or sun.

lessons.title: Farmhouses in Europe
lessons.mainIdea: Farm families build homes that fit their fields, animals, and weather.
reading: Anna lives on a farm in the mountains of Switzerland. Her house has a big, steep roof. In winter, lots of snow falls. The snow slides off the steep roof.
Anna's family keeps cows. The barn is close to the house. In some old farmhouses, the house and barn were under one roof. That made chores easier in the snow.
Farmhouses in other parts of Europe look different. Some are stone. Some are wood. Each one fits its land and weather.

words.d: a home on a farm where a farm family lives
what the air is like outside, such as hot, cold, rainy, or snowy

look.title: Two Roofs
look.text: Look at two houses. One has a flat roof. Snow piles on top, higher and higher. The other has a steep roof like a tall tent. Snow slides off and falls to the ground.
look.prompt: Which roof is better for a snowy place? Why?

check.q: Why does Anna's house have a steep roof?
check.why: The reading says lots of snow falls, and it slides off the steep roof.

check.q: In some old farmhouses, what was under one roof?
check.why: The reading says some old farmhouses had the house and barn under one roof.

check.q: What is true about farmhouses in Europe?
choices: They are all made of snow
Each one fits its land and weather
check.why: The reading says some are stone and some are wood. Each fits its land and weather.

lessons.title: What Every Home Needs
lessons.mainIdea: Every home gives shelter, warmth, and water, and people who care.
reading: A ger, an apartment, and a stilt house look very different. But they all do the same big jobs. They keep people safe from wind, rain, and cold.
A home gives *shelter*. It helps people stay warm or cool. It needs clean water close by. It is a place to eat, rest, and sleep.
Most of all, a home is where people care for each other. Bat felt safe in the new place. His family was with him. That made it home.

words.d: a place that keeps you safe from wind, rain, cold, or sun
the place where you live and where people care for you

look.title: A World Promise About Homes
look.text: Everyone has the right to a standard of living adequate for the health and well-being of himself and of his family, including food, clothing, housing and medical care.
look.cite: United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 25, 1948
look.prompt: Find the word housing. What does this promise say every family should have?

check.q: What big job do all homes do?
choices: Keep people safe from wind, rain, and cold
check.why: The reading says homes that look different all keep people safe from wind, rain, and cold.

check.q: Which thing does a home need close by?
check.why: The reading says a home needs clean water close by.

check.q: Why did the new place feel like home to Bat?
check.why: The reading says his family was with him. That made it home.

review.q: Which home can a family take with them when they move?
review.why: A ger can be taken down and put up again, so herders take it with them.

review.q: Why are some houses in Thailand built on stilts?
choices: To stay dry when water rises
review.why: Stilts hold the house above the water in the rainy season.

review.q: Which home fits a hot, dry place best?
choices: An adobe house with thick walls
review.why: Thick adobe walls keep the inside cool in hot, dry places like New Mexico.

review.q: Why do big cities like Tokyo and New York have many apartments?
choices: Many people and not much land
review.why: Cities have lots of people and little land, so they build up.
Long ago, some Inuit hunters built snow-block shelters in winter.

review.q: What makes a place a home most of all?
choices: People who care for each other
review.why: The chapter says a home is where people care for each other.
